¶
'''Weather Bureau''', a bureau of the Department of Agriculture, having charge of the forecasting of weather, the issue of storm-warnings, the display of weather- and flood-signals, the gaging and reporting of rivers, the maintenance of sea-coast telegraph-lines, the collection and transmission of marine intelligence for the benefit of commerce and navigation, the taking of meteorological observations for establishing the climatic conditions of the United States, and the distribution of meteorological information. From 1871 to 1891 these duties were performe by the signal service of the army, which during that per was popularly called the ''Weather Bureau.''—'''Weath signal.''' See ''signal.''

'''II.''' ''a. Naut.'', toward the wind; windwa opposed to ''lee:'' as, ''weather'' bow; ''weather'' be ''weather'' rigging.—'''Weather anchor''', the ancho ing to windward, by which a ship rides when moor '''Weather helm, quarter, tide.''' See the nouns.

'''weather''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr), ''v.'' [< ME. ''wederen'', < ''wederian'', ''wedrian'', expose to the air, indicate weather; cf. AS. ''wedrian'' = Sw. ''vädra'', exp to the air, air, scent, smell, snuff the air, = Da ''vejre'', air, scent; from the noun.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To air; expose to the air; dry or otherwise affect by exposure to the open air. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|I fear me this land is not yet ripe to be ploughed; for, as the saying is, it lacketh ''weathering.''
{{right|''Latimer'', Sermon of the Plougl}}
<poem>And then he pearcheth on some braunch thereby,
To ''weather'' him, and his moyst wings to dry.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Muiopotmos, l. 1}}}}

{{smaller block|His head . . . looked like a ''weather-cock'', perched upon his spindle neck to tell which way the wind blew.
{{right|''Irving'', Sketch-Book, p. 420.}}}}
'''2.''' Figuratively, any thing or person that is easily and frequently turned or swayed; a fickle or inconstant person.
{{smaller block|What pretty ''weathercocks'' these women are!
{{right|''Randolph'', Amyntas, i. 1.}}
<poem>The word which I have given shall stand like fate,
Not like the king’s, that ''weather-cock'' of state.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Conquest of Granada, I., iii. 1.}}}}

'''weathercock''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-kok), ''v. t.'' [< ''weathercock'', ''n.''] To serve as a weathercock to or on. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Whose blazing wyvern ''weathercock’d'' the spire.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Aylmer’s Field.}}}}

'''weather-contact''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-kon″takt), ''n.'' In ''teleg.'', leakage to neighboring wires or to earth, due to wet insulators.

'''weather-cross''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-krôs), ''n.'' In telegraph- and telephone-lines, a leakage from one line to another, caused by poor insulation, and brought about by wet or stormy weather.

'''weather-dog''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-dog), ''n.'' A fragmentary rainbow, popularly believed, especially in Cornwall, to be an indication of rain. [Prov. Eng.]

'''weather-driven''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-driv″n), ''a.'' [= Sw. ''vädrifven'', wind-driven; as ''weather'' + ''driven''.] Driven by winds or storms; forced by stress of weather.

'''weathered''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėrd), ''p. a.'' '''1.''' Discolored or disintegrated by the action of the elements:

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader||6862|weathered}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|{{right|''York Plays'', p. 114.}}}}
{{smaller block|ey . . . wolde ride in the cole of the mornynge that was feire and stille and a softe ''weder'', and thei were yonge and tender to suffre grete trauayle.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 191.}}}}

{{smaller block|Gentlewomen, the ''weather'''s hot; whither walk you?
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Bartholomew Fair, iii. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|Horrible ''weather'' again to-day, snowing and raining all day.
{{right|''Sydney Smith'', To Mrs. Sydney Smith.}}}}

'''5.''' Specifically, in weather-maps and -reports, the condition of the sky as to cloudiness and the occurrence of precipitation.—'''6.''' Change of the state of the atmosphere; meteorological change; hence, figuratively, vicissitude; change of fortune or condition.

{{smaller block|It is a reverend thing to see an ancient castle . . . not in decay; how much more to behold an ancient noble family which hath stood against the waves and ''weathers'' of time!
{{right|''Bacon'', Nobility.}}}}

<poem>But my Substantial Love
Of a more firm and perfect Nature is;
No ''Weathers'' can it move.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Cowley'', The Mistress, Coldness.}}}}

'''7.''' The inclination or obliquity of the sails of a windmill to the plane of revolution.—'''Angle of weather.''' {{smaller|See ''angle''<sup>3</sup>.}}—'''Clerk of the weather.''' {{smaller|See ''clerk''.}}—'''Merry weather†.''' {{smaller|See ''merry''<sup>1</sup>.}}—'''Soft weather.''' {{smaller|(''a'') A thaw. [New Eng.] (''b'') An enervating atmosphere.}}—'''To make fair weather†''', {{smaller|to conciliate or flatter, as by fair words and shows of friendship.}}

<poem>I must ''make fair weather'' yet awhile,
Till Henry be more weak and I more strong.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., v. 1. 30.}}}}

'''To make good''' {{smaller|or}} '''bad weather''' {{smaller|(''naut'').}} {{smaller|See ''make''<sup>1</sup>.}}—'''Under the weather''', {{smaller|indisposed; ill; ailing: a condition caused or influenced by the state of the weather. [Colloq.]}}

{{smaller block|Since I went to Washington, and until within ten days, I have been quite ''under the weather'', and I have had to neglect everything.
{{right|''S. Bowles'', in Merriam, II. 49.}}}}

From 1871 to 1891 these duties were performe by the signal service of the army, which during that per was popularly called the ''Weather Bureau.''—'''Weath signal.''' See ''signal.''

'''weather''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr), ''v.''   [< ME. ''wederen'', < ''wederian'', ''wedrian'', expose to the air, indicate weather; cf. AS. ''wedrian'' = Sw. ''vädra'', exp to the air, air, scent, smell, snuff the air, = Da ''vejre'', air, scent; from the noun.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To air; expose to the air; dry or otherwise affect by exposure to the open air. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|I fear me this land is not yet ripe to be ploughed; for, as the saying is, it lacketh ''weathering.''
{{right|''Latimer'', Sermon of the Plougl}}}}

To ''weather'' him, and his moyst wings to dry.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Muiopotmos, l. 1}}}}
{{smaller block|have got mow-burnt or musty in the stack, should be rigidly rejected. {{right|''Ure'', Dict., III. 185.}}}}

{{smaller block|Hawks are ''weathered'' by being placed unhooded in the open air. This term is applied to passage hawks which are not sufficiently reclaimed to be left out by themselves unhooded on blocks—they are ''weathered'' by being put out for an hour or two under the falconer’s eye.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', IX. 7.}}}}

'''2.''' To affect injuriously by the action of weather; in ''geol.'', to discolor or disintegrate: as, the atmospheric agencies that ''weather'' rocks. —'''3.''' In ''tile-manuf.'', to expose (the clay) to a hot sun or to frost, in order to open the pores and separate the particles, that it may readily absorb water and be easily worked.—'''4.''' To slope (a surface), that it may shed water.—'''5.''' ''Naut.'': (''a'') To sail to windward of: as, to ''weather'' a point or cape.

{{smaller block|We ''weathered'' Pulo Pare on the 29th, and stood in for the main. {{right|''Cook'', First Voyage, iii. 13.}}}}

(''b'') To bear up against and come safely through: said of a ship in a storm, as also of a mariner; hence, used in the same sense with reference to storms on land.

{{smaller block|Here ’s to the pilot that ''weathered'' the storm. {{right|''Canning.''}}}}
<poem>Among these hills, from first to last,
We’ve ''weathered'' many a furious blast.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Wordsworth'', The Waggoner, ii.}}}}
{{smaller block|I ''weathered'' some weary snow-storms.
{{right|''Thoreau'', Walden, p. 275.}}}}
<poem>To sell the boat—and yet he loved her well;
How many a rough sea had he ''weather’d'' in her!</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson'', Enoch Arden.}}}}

'''6.''' Figuratively, to bear up against and overcome, as trouble or danger; come out of, as a trial, without permanent damage or loss.
{{smaller block|You will ''weather'' the difficulties yet. {{right|''F. W. Robertson.''}}}}
{{smaller block|The vitality and self-direction of the semi-Greek municipalities of the East in large measure ''weathered'' Roman rule, as did also the Greek speech and partially Hellenized life of Asia, Syria, and Egypt. {{right|''W. Wilson'', State, § 143.}}}}
'''To weather a point''', {{smaller|to gain an advantage or accomplish a purpose against opposition.}}—'''To weather out''', {{smaller|to hold out against to the end.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>When we have pass’d these gloomy hours,
And ''weather’d out'' the storm that beats upon us.</poem>
{{right|''Addison'', Cato, iii. 2.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To suffer a change, such as discoloration or more or less complete disintegration, in consequence of exposure to the weather or atmosphere. See ''weathering'', 2.
{{smaller block|The lowest bed is a sandstone with ferruginous veins; it ''weathers'' into an extraordinary honey-combed mass. {{right|''Darwin'', Geol. Observations, ii. 426.}}}}
{{smaller block|The granite commenced to ''weather'', and ''weathered'' merrily on in spite of all technical and scientific commissions. {{right|''Science'', VII. 75.}}}}
'''2.''' To resist or bear exposure to the weather.
{{smaller block|For outside work, boiled oil is used, because it ''weathers'' better than raw oil. {{right|''Workshop Receipts'', 2d ser., p. 436.}}}}

'''weather-beaten''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-bē″tn), ''a.''   [< ''weather'' + ''beaten''. In some of its uses perhaps a perverted spelling of ''weather-bitten'', q. v.]   Beaten or marred by the weather; seasoned or hardened by exposure to all kinds of weather: as, a ''weather-beaten'' sailor.
{{smaller block|<poem>She enjoyes sure peace for evermore,
As ''wetherbeaten'' ship arryv’d on happie shore.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Summer being ended, all things stand in appearance with a ''weather-beaten'' face.
{{right|''N. Morton'', New England’s Memorial, p. 35.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''weather-beaten'' form of the scout.
{{right|''J. F. Cooper'', Last of Mohicans, xxix.}}}}

'''weather-bitt''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-bit), ''v. t.'' To take an rn off rain, snow, etc.
{{smaller block|It was a building of four rooms, constructed of hewn gs and ''weather-boarded'' at the joints.
{{right|''The Century'', XXXVIII. 408.}}}}

'''eather-boarding''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-bōr″ding), ''n.'' '''1.''' facing of thin boards, having usually a feaer-edge, and nailed lapping one over another, sed as an outside covering for the walls of wooden building. They are practically the me as clapboards, but are distinguished from ose by being larger and wider.—'''2.''' The finish woodwork at the base of a clapboarded all.—'''3.''' The whole exterior covering of a all or roof, whether of weather-boards, clapards, or shingles.—'''Weather-boarding clamp, ge, saw,''' {{smaller|etc., special forms of ''clamp, gage, saw,'' etc., ed in applying or cutting out weather-boarding.}}

'''ather-bound''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-bound), ''a.'' Delayed bad weather.

'''ather-box''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-boks), ''n.'' A form of groscope, in the shape of a toy-house, which ughly indicates weather changes by the aparance or retirement of toy images. {{smaller|In a comn form a man advances from his porch in wet and a oman in dry weather—the movement being produced by varying torsion of a hygroscopic string by which the ages are attached. Also called ''weather-house''.}}
{{smaller block|The elder and younger son of the house of Crawley were, e the gentleman and lady in the ''weather-box'', never at me together.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Vanity Fair, x.}}}}
